title: A/B test models in production
gist: Together AI details endpoint-level A/B experiments that split live LLM traffic into one control plus up to 20 variants with fixed percentage shares, letting teams measure real-user quality (not just shadow-traffic operational health) and promote winners via blue-green rollout. A live demo ramping 95/5 to 80/20 to 50/50 shows observed shares tracking configured percents within a point, with ~30-60s propagation and clean unwinding on delete.

insights.claim: Shadow traffic cannot answer whether a new model is better for users because shadowed responses are discarded and no user ever acts on them; only real exposure measures quality signals like retention and task completion.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Teams relying on shadow tests for quality decisions are measuring the wrong thing and need live-exposure experiments.
insights.quote: Shadowing tells you the candidate is operationally sound with respect to latency, errors, throughput, but its responses are discarded; no user ever acts on them.

insights.claim: Home-built A/B testing via feature flags, hash-mod-100 on user ID, and hardcoded model strings entangles experiments with infrastructure, causing cohort drift from client caching and branching code that outlives the experiment.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: The maintenance and drift cost of DIY experimentation is the pain Together's endpoint-level design targets.
insights.quote: even after the experiment "ends" the branching code lives on long afterward because nobody's sure it's safe to remove.

insights.claim: Together AI runs A/B experiment logic at the endpoint level, so clients see the same endpoint name, API, and keys while a set percentage of requests is answered by the variant.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Moving experiment logic out of app code eliminates client-side routing changes and unwind risk.
insights.locator: run A/B experiment logic at the endpoint level

insights.claim: An A/B experiment attaches to an endpoint with exactly one control and one or more variants whose percents must sum to 100, and the experiment subdivides the control's share of base traffic.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Understanding that percents are absolute shares of control traffic is essential to configuring valid experiments.

insights.claim: Variant deployments must carry zero weight and stay out of the endpoint's base traffic split, because if a variant also drew capacity-weighted traffic the measurements would be quietly wrong.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Misconfiguring variant weight silently corrupts experiment results, so setup discipline is a data-integrity requirement.
insights.quote: If a variant could also draw capacity-weighted traffic from the split, your measurements would be quietly wrong.

insights.claim: A/B percents are true fixed traffic shares summing to 100% and are independent of replica counts, deliberately different from traffic-split weights which are per-ready-replica and follow capacity.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Fixed shares keep the measurement constant so results don't drift with autoscaling during the test.
insights.quote: An experiment is a measurement instrument; you want the split to be constant while you measure and not drift with autoscaling.
insights.locator: A/B percents are true fixed traffic shares

insights.claim: A control whose split weight is zero gives the experiment nothing to subdivide, so the whole experiment receives no traffic.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: An edge case that would silently zero out an experiment if the control is misconfigured.
insights.locator: control whose split weight is zero

insights.claim: Together frames three canonical splits: 95/5 for a new model's first exposure (slow signal, minimal risk), 80/20 for a more significant readout after surviving 5%, and 50/50 for fastest signal in late-stage confirmation between two known-good options.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: A ready-made decision table for trading signal speed against blast radius when rolling out models.

insights.claim: The platform supports up to 20 variant members for multi-way tests, such as running a full-precision endpoint against three quantized variants, as long as percents sum to 100% with exactly one control.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Multi-arm capacity lets teams compare quantization levels in a single production experiment.

insights.claim: Every request is served by a specific deployment and every platform metric is available per deployment, so the deployment ID is the join key linking infra metrics to product-side quality signals the team logs itself.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Trivial attribution via deployment ID means teams own the quality judgment while infra comparison is free.
insights.quote: The platform deliberately doesn't guess at your quality metrics; it makes the attribution trivial so your analytics can do the judging.

insights.claim: Cohort assignment uses the request's sampling key such as a top-level prompt_cache_key or user field, so requests with the same key route consistently and a user can stay in one arm across a session; keyless requests are assigned at random per request.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Multi-turn quality studies require a stable user field to keep users in one arm, or per-turn randomization skews results.

insights.claim: There is no separate ramp API; an update replaces the full member list and is guarded by an etag so a teammate's concurrent ramp is rejected rather than silently overwritten.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Etag concurrency control prevents two operators from silently clobbering each other's traffic changes.
insights.locator: Ramping is resending the member set

insights.claim: Ending a winning experiment is two steps: promote via a blue-green rollout from control to variant with health gates and rollback safety, then delete the experiment so 100% of traffic follows the post-rollout base split.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: The promote-then-delete pattern lets winners ship without leaving branching code behind.

insights.claim: A degraded variant's blast radius is limited to its own cohort because deployments are independently monitored and autoscaled, which is a key reason to start experiments at 5%.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Independent isolation means a bad candidate can't drag down the control, bounding downside risk.
insights.quote: a struggling variant won’t drag the control down.

insights.claim: In a live-endpoint run at a steady 3 RPS, observed traffic shares tracked configured percents closely: 95.3/4.7 at 95/5 over 1,330 requests, 79.2/20.8 at 80/20, 50.2/49.8 at 50/50, and 100/0 after delete.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Empirical proof that configured splits materialize accurately over meaningful volume, validating the instrument.

insights.claim: Routing changes propagate fast but not instantly; the demo waited ~75 seconds after each update and the routing layer picks up experiment changes on the same 30-60s timescale as traffic-split changes.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Operators must allow ~30-60s propagation before trusting post-change measurements.
insights.locator: Propagation is fast but not instant

insights.claim: After removing the experiment, 360 consecutive requests all landed on the control with no leftover cohort logic to unwind.
insights.speaker: Together AI Blog
insights.so_what: Clean teardown removes the maintenance debt that plagues app-layer experiments.

source_meta.author: Zain Hasan, Zarni Phyo, Nikitha Suryadevara, Ted Cui
